lesson.title: Whole Numbers and Place Value
lesson.summary: Read, write, compare and round big numbers, and solve word problems.
objectives: Name the place and the value of a digit
Write a number in expanded form
Round numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1,000
Solve addition, subtraction, multiplication and division word problems
lesson.html:
1. Place value

Every digit in a number has a place (where it stands) and a value (how much it is worth). Moving one place to the left makes a digit ten times bigger.

Example: In 462,805 the digit 6 is in the ten thousands place, so its value is 6 × 10,000 = 60,000.

2. Expanded form

Write the value of each digit and add them: 462,805 = 400,000 + 60,000 + 2,000 + 800 + 5 (zeros are left out).

3. Rounding off

  1. Find the place you are rounding to.
  2. Look at the digit to its right.
  3. If it is 5 or more, add 1 to the rounding digit (round up). If it is less than 5, keep it (round down).
  4. Replace all digits to the right with zeros.

Example: Round 49,530 to the nearest hundred. The digit after the hundreds place (5) is 3, which is less than 5, so we round down: 49,500.

4. Comparing numbers

Compare the number of digits first. If they are the same, compare digit by digit from the left. Use > (greater than) and < (less than).

5. Word problems

  • Altogether / total → add.
  • How many left / difference → subtract.
  • Each costs ... how much for many → multiply.
  • Share equally → divide.

Worked example: A trader buys 24 books at ₦350 each. Total = 24 × 350 = ₦8,400.

Common Entrance tip: Always write the working. Check your answer by doing the opposite operation.

topics.title: Reading and writing large numbers
topics.note: Read a big number in groups of three digits from the right: units, thousands, millions. Say each group, then its name. Example: 462,805 is four hundred and sixty-two thousand, eight hundred and five.
steps: Split the number into groups of three digits from the right (units, thousands, millions).
Read each group as a number, then say its name (thousand, million).
Write "and" before the last tens or units part.
To write in figures, place each group and fill empty places with 0.
topics.mistake: Forgetting zeros: "three thousand and five" is 3,005, not 3,5.

topics.title: Place value of whole numbers
topics.note: Each digit has a place and a value. Moving one place left makes the value 10 times bigger. In 4,672 the digit 6 is in the hundreds place, so its value is 600.
steps: Write the number in a place value chart (units, tens, hundreds, thousands ...).
Find the digit and read the column name: that is its place.
Value = digit × the value of its place.
A zero holds a place but has no value.
topics.mistake: Mixing "place" (hundreds) with "value" (600). Place is the name, value is the amount.

topics.title: Skip counting in large numbers
topics.note: Find the step (the number added or subtracted each time) by subtracting two neighbouring numbers. Then keep adding the same step. Example: 2,500; 5,000; 7,500 goes up by 2,500.
steps: Subtract two neighbouring numbers to find the step.
Check the step is the same everywhere.
Add the step to find the next term; subtract to go back.
For the nth term, multiply the step by n (when counting from zero).
topics.mistake: Adding the wrong step. Always check with two different pairs.

topics.title: Addition of whole numbers
topics.note: Line up the digits by place value and add from the right, carrying 1 to the next column when a column adds up to 10 or more. Check by adding in the opposite order.
steps: Write the numbers one under the other with units under units.
Add the units column first, then tens, hundreds, and so on.
If a column is 10 or more, write the units digit and carry the tens to the next column.
Check by adding in reverse order.
topics.mistake: Not lining up the digits, so tens get added to units.

topics.title: Subtraction of whole numbers
topics.note: Line up the digits and subtract from the right, borrowing 10 from the next column when the top digit is smaller. Check by adding your answer to the number you subtracted.
steps: Write the bigger number on top and line up the digits.
Subtract each column from the right.
If the top digit is smaller, borrow 10 from the next column (that column drops by 1).
Check: answer + smaller number = bigger number.
topics.mistake: Subtracting the smaller digit from the bigger one in each column, even when the bigger digit is on the bottom.

topics.title: Addition of decimal fractions
topics.note: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same decimal places, then add as for whole numbers. Put the point straight down in the answer.
steps: Write the numbers so the decimal points are in a straight line.
Fill empty places with zeros (2.5 becomes 2.50).
Add as whole numbers from the right.
Bring the decimal point straight down.
topics.mistake: Lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points.

topics.title: Subtraction of decimal fractions
topics.note: Line up the decimal points, add zeros where needed, then subtract as for whole numbers. Put the point straight down in the answer.
steps: Add zeros so both numbers have the same number of decimal places.
Subtract from the right, borrowing when needed.
Bring the decimal point straight down.
topics.mistake: Forgetting zeros: 5 − 2.35 is 5.00 − 2.35 = 2.65.

topics.title: Multiplication of whole numbers
topics.note: Multiply by each digit of the bottom number, starting from the right. Add a zero for the tens row, two zeros for the hundreds row, then add the rows.
steps: Multiply the top number by the units digit of the bottom number.
Put a 0 under the units and multiply by the tens digit (two zeros for hundreds).
Add the rows to get the answer.
Estimate first to check it is sensible.
topics.mistake: Forgetting to add the zero for the tens row.

topics.title: Multiplication of decimal fractions
topics.note: Ignore the decimal points and multiply as whole numbers. Then count the total decimal places in both numbers and give the answer that many places. Example: 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06.
steps: Ignore the decimal points and multiply as whole numbers.
Count the decimal places in both numbers together.
Put the point in the answer so it has that many places.
To multiply by 10, 100, 1,000 move the point 1, 2, 3 places right.
topics.mistake: Putting the point in the wrong place. 0.4 × 0.3 = 0.12 (two places), not 1.2.

topics.title: Squares of numbers
topics.note: The square of a number is the number multiplied by itself. $7^2 = 7 × 7 = 49$. Square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.
steps: For area of a square: side × side.
topics.mistake: Doubling instead of squaring: $6^2 = 36$, not 12.

topics.title: Square roots of numbers
topics.note: The square root undoes squaring. $\sqrt{49} = 7$ because $7 × 7 = 49$. Learn the squares up to 15 × 15 so square roots are quick.
steps: Ask: which number multiplied by itself gives this?
Use the list of squares you know.
topics.mistake: Halving instead of finding the root: $\sqrt{36} = 6$, not 18.

topics.title: Division of whole numbers
topics.note: Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down the next digit and repeat. What is left at the end is the remainder. Check: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend.
steps: Divide the first digits, write the answer on top.
Multiply the answer by the divisor and subtract.
Bring down the next digit and repeat.
What is left at the end is the remainder.
topics.mistake: Forgetting to bring down a digit, or forgetting a zero in the answer.

topics.title: Division of decimal fractions
topics.note: To divide by a whole number, divide normally and keep the point in the same place. To divide by 10, 100 or 1,000, move the point 1, 2 or 3 places to the left.
steps: If dividing by a whole number, divide normally and put the point straight up.
To divide by 10, 100, 1,000 move the point 1, 2, 3 places left.
Add zeros after the point when you run out of digits.
topics.mistake: Moving the point the wrong way. Dividing makes the number smaller.

topics.title: Factors of numbers
topics.note: A factor divides a number exactly. Find factors in pairs: for 12: 1 × 12, 2 × 6, 3 × 4, so the factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
steps: Start with 1 and the number itself.
Test 2, 3, 4, 5 ... to see if each divides exactly.
topics.mistake: Leaving out 1 or the number itself.

topics.title: Multiples of numbers
topics.note: Multiples are the answers in a times table. Multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35 ... A number is always a multiple of itself.
steps: A multiple is always as big as, or bigger than, the number.
To test: divide; if there is no remainder it is a multiple.
topics.mistake: Mixing multiples (bigger) with factors (smaller).

topics.title: Prime factors
topics.note: A prime number has exactly two factors (2, 3, 5, 7, 11 ...). Divide repeatedly by primes. Example: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
steps: Divide by the smallest prime (2) as many times as you can.
Write the primes as a product, e.g. 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
topics.mistake: Using non-prime numbers like 4 or 9 in the final answer.

topics.title: Highest Common Factor
topics.note: The HCF is the biggest number that divides all the given numbers exactly. List factors or use prime factors. HCF of 12 and 18 is 6.
steps: List the factors of each number (or use prime factors).
Circle the factors found in every list.
The biggest circled factor is the HCF.
Use the HCF to simplify fractions and to share into equal groups.
topics.mistake: Confusing HCF (a factor, smaller) with LCM (a multiple, bigger).

topics.title: Lowest Common Multiple
topics.note: The LCM is the smallest number that all the given numbers divide into. List multiples until one appears in every list. LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.
steps: Find the first multiple that is in every list.
Use the LCM to find common denominators and repeating events.
topics.mistake: Multiplying the numbers together, which may not be the smallest.

lesson.title: Fractions
lesson.summary: Equivalent fractions, simplifying, adding, subtracting, mixed numbers and fractions of amounts.
objectives: Add and subtract fractions with different denominators
Change between mixed numbers and improper fractions
Find a fraction of an amount
lesson.html:
1. What is a fraction?

A fraction shows part of a whole. The bottom number (denominator) tells how many equal parts the whole is cut into. The top number (numerator) tells how many parts we take.

3 of the 4 equal parts are shaded, so the fraction is 3/4.

2. Equivalent fractions

Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8.

3. Simplest form

Divide the top and bottom by their highest common factor (HCF). 12/18: HCF is 6, so 12/18 = 2/3.

4. Adding and subtracting

  1. Find the LCM of the denominators.
  2. Change each fraction to that denominator.
  3. Add or subtract the numerators. Keep the denominator.
  4. Simplify.

Example: 1/3 + 1/4. LCM of 3 and 4 is 12. 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.

5. Mixed numbers and improper fractions

2 3/5 = (2 × 5 + 3)/5 = 13/5. To go back, divide: 13 ÷ 5 = 2 remainder 3, so 2 3/5.

6. Fraction of an amount

Divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. 3/5 of ₦400 = (400 ÷ 5) × 3 = 80 × 3 = ₦240.

Common Entrance tip: A fraction with the same top and bottom equals 1. Always simplify your final answer.

topics.title: Decimals
topics.note: A decimal point separates whole numbers from parts. After the point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. To compare decimals, compare digit by digit from the left.
steps: Whole numbers are left of the point, parts are right of it.
First place after the point is tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths.
To compare, line up the points and compare digit by digit from the left.
Adding zeros at the end of a decimal does not change its value.
topics.mistake: Thinking 0.45 is bigger than 0.5 because 45 is bigger than 5.

topics.title: Conversion of fractions to decimals
topics.note: Divide the top by the bottom. $\frac{3}{4} = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75$. For a mixed number, keep the whole number and convert the fraction part.
steps: Divide the numerator by the denominator.
Add a decimal point and zeros to keep dividing.
For a mixed number, keep the whole number and convert the fraction.
topics.mistake: Dividing the denominator by the numerator (the wrong way round).

topics.title: Conversion of decimals to fractions
topics.note: Write the decimal digits over 10, 100 or 1,000 (one, two or three places) and simplify. $0.35 = \frac{35}{100} = \frac{7}{20}$.
steps: Simplify by dividing top and bottom by their HCF.
A whole-number part becomes a mixed number.
topics.mistake: Not simplifying the final fraction.

topics.title: Addition of fractions
topics.note: Make the denominators the same (use the LCM), add the numerators, keep the denominator, then simplify. $\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{4}{12} + \frac{3}{12} = \frac{7}{12}$.
steps: Find the LCM of the denominators.
Change each fraction to that denominator.
Add the numerators and keep the denominator.
Simplify and change to a mixed number if needed.
topics.mistake: Adding the denominators too: $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}$ is not $\frac{2}{5}$.

topics.title: Subtraction of fractions
topics.note: Make the denominators the same, subtract the numerators, keep the denominator, then simplify. $\frac{3}{4} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{9}{12} - \frac{2}{12} = \frac{7}{12}$.
steps: Find the LCM of the denominators.
Change each fraction to that denominator.
Subtract the numerators; keep the denominator.
topics.mistake: Subtracting the denominators as well.

topics.title: Multiplication of fractions
topics.note: Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms, then simplify. Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first. $\frac{2}{3} × \frac{3}{5} = \frac{6}{15} = \frac{2}{5}$.
steps: Change any mixed numbers to improper fractions.
Cancel common factors across the top and bottom if you can.
Multiply tops together and bottoms together.
topics.mistake: Finding a common denominator first (not needed for multiplying).

topics.title: Division of fractions
topics.note: Flip the second fraction (find its reciprocal) and multiply. $\frac{1}{2} ÷ \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2} × \frac{4}{1} = 2$.
steps: Flip the second fraction upside down.
topics.mistake: Flipping the first fraction instead of the second.

lesson.title: Percentages
lesson.summary: Percent of an amount, converting, increase and decrease, discount, profit and loss.
objectives: Find a percentage of an amount
Increase and decrease an amount by a percentage
lesson.html:
1. Meaning of percent

Percent means "out of 100". 25% = 25/100 = 1/4.

2. Converting

  • Fraction → percent: multiply by 100%. 3/5 × 100% = 60%.
  • Percent → fraction: write over 100 and simplify. 40% = 40/100 = 2/5.

3. Percentage of an amount

Write the percent as a fraction over 100 and multiply. 20% of ₦1,500 = 20/100 × 1,500 = ₦300.

4. Increase and decrease

Find the percentage, then add (increase) or subtract (decrease). Price ₦800 increased by 25%: 25% of 800 = 200, new price = 800 + 200 = ₦1,000.

5. Discount

Discount is the amount taken off the price. A ₦2,000 shirt with 10% discount: discount = ₦200, you pay ₦2,000 − ₦200 = ₦1,800.

6. Profit and loss percent

Profit = Selling price − Cost price.
Profit % = (Profit ÷ Cost price) × 100%.
Bought for ₦4,000 and sold for ₦5,000: profit = ₦1,000, profit % = 1,000/4,000 × 100% = 25%.

Common Entrance tip: Profit and loss percent are always worked on the cost price.

topics.title: Conversion of fractions to percentages
topics.note: Multiply the fraction by 100%. $\frac{3}{5} × 100\% = 60\%$.
steps: Or divide top by bottom to get a decimal, then × 100.
topics.mistake: Forgetting the % sign or multiplying by 10.

topics.title: Conversion of percentages to fractions
topics.note: Write the percent over 100 and simplify. $45\% = \frac{45}{100} = \frac{9}{20}$.
steps: Simplify by dividing top and bottom by the HCF.
For decimals like 12.5%, multiply top and bottom by 10 first.
topics.mistake: Leaving the fraction unsimplified.

topics.title: Conversion of decimals to percentages
topics.note: Multiply by 100 (move the point two places right). $0.37 = 37\%$.
steps: That means move the point two places to the right.
topics.mistake: Moving the point only one place.

topics.title: Conversion of percentages to decimals
topics.note: Divide by 100 (move the point two places left). $8\% = 0.08$.
steps: That means move the point two places to the left.
topics.mistake: Writing 8% as 0.8.

topics.title: Order of operations
topics.note: Use BODMAS: Brackets, Orders (powers), Division and Multiplication (left to right), Addition and Subtraction (left to right). $2 + 3 × 4 = 14$, not 20.
steps: D and M: Division and Multiplication, left to right.
A and S: Addition and Subtraction, left to right.
topics.mistake: Working left to right without BODMAS: $2+3×4$ is 14, not 20.

topics.title: Scale drawing
topics.note: A scale compares drawing length with real length. If 1 cm stands for 5 m, then 8 cm on the drawing is 40 m in real life. Multiply to go real, divide to go back to the drawing.
steps: Read the scale: 1 cm stands for ___ real units.
Use the same units on both sides.
topics.mistake: Multiplying when you should divide (or the reverse).

topics.title: Rounding off whole numbers
topics.note: Look at the digit just right of the place you round to. 5 or more: round up. Less than 5: keep. Then replace the digits after with zeros.
steps: Find the place you are rounding to.
Look at the digit to its right.
5 or more: add 1 to the rounding digit. Less than 5: leave it.
Change all digits after it to zeros.
topics.mistake: Rounding up the wrong digit or forgetting the zeros.

topics.title: Rounding off decimal numbers
topics.note: To round to a number of decimal places, look at the next digit. 5 or more: round up. Less than 5: keep the digit. 3.456 to 2 d.p. is 3.46.
steps: Count to the decimal place you need.
5 or more: round up; less than 5: leave it.
Drop the digits after the place.
topics.mistake: Looking at the wrong digit.

topics.title: Estimation of numbers
topics.note: Round each number first, then calculate. Estimate 48 × 21: 50 × 20 = 1,000. Use estimates to check your answers are sensible.
steps: Round each number to an easy number (nearest 10, 100, 1,000).
Do the calculation with the rounded numbers.
Compare your estimate with the exact answer.
An estimate should be close, not exact.
topics.mistake: Rounding too much, which gives an estimate far from the answer.

topics.title: Ratio
topics.note: A ratio compares quantities. Simplify by dividing by the HCF. To share in a ratio, add the parts, find one part, then multiply. Share 60 in the ratio 1 : 2 → one part is 20, so 20 and 40.
steps: Write the quantities in the order given.
Divide both by their HCF to simplify.
To share: add the parts, find one part, multiply.
Make sure both quantities use the same units.
topics.mistake: Writing the ratio in the wrong order (boys : girls is not girls : boys).

topics.title: Proportion
topics.note: Two ratios that are equal form a proportion: $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$. Cross-multiply to find a missing number: $a × d = b × c$.
steps: Write the two equal ratios as fractions.
Check that both ratios simplify to the same thing.
topics.mistake: Cross-multiplying wrongly (top with top).

topics.title: Direct proportion
topics.note: When one quantity increases, the other increases at the same rate. Find the value of one unit, then multiply. 5 books cost ₦2,000, so 1 costs ₦400 and 8 cost ₦3,200.
steps: Find the value of ONE unit (divide).
Multiply by the number you want.
Check: more items should cost more.
Write the units in the answer.
topics.mistake: Using subtraction instead of the unit value.

topics.title: Inverse proportion
topics.note: When one quantity increases, the other decreases. The product stays the same. 4 men take 6 days: total work = 24 man-days, so 8 men take 24 ÷ 8 = 3 days.
steps: Find the total work: workers × days.
Divide the total by the new number of workers.
Check: more workers means fewer days.
Same idea for speed and time.
topics.mistake: Treating it as direct proportion (more workers, more days).

topics.title: Percentage increase
topics.note: Find the percentage of the amount, then add it. Increase ₦800 by 25%: 25% of 800 = 200, new amount = ₦1,000. Percentage increase = increase ÷ original × 100%.
steps: Find the percentage of the original amount.
Add it to the original amount.
topics.mistake: Working the percentage on the new amount instead of the original.

topics.title: Percentage decrease
topics.note: Find the percentage of the amount, then subtract it. Decrease ₦800 by 25%: 25% of 800 = 200, new amount = ₦600. Percentage decrease = decrease ÷ original × 100%.
steps: Find the percentage of the original amount.
topics.mistake: Adding instead of subtracting.

topics.title: Profit and loss
topics.note: Profit = Selling price − Cost price (when SP is more). Loss = Cost price − Selling price. Profit % = profit ÷ cost price × 100%.
steps: Compare Selling price (SP) and Cost price (CP).
SP more than CP: profit = SP − CP. CP more than SP: loss = CP − SP.
% profit or loss = (profit or loss ÷ CP) × 100%.
Always work on the cost price.
topics.mistake: Using the selling price as the base for the percentage.

topics.title: Simple interest
topics.note: Interest $I = \frac{P × R × T}{100}$ where P is the principal, R the rate per year and T the years. Amount = Principal + Interest.
steps: Identify P (money), R (rate % per year), T (years).
To find R or T, rearrange the formula.
topics.mistake: Forgetting to divide by 100 or mixing months with years.

topics.title: Discount
topics.note: Discount is the amount taken off the marked price. Discount = percent × price. Sale price = marked price − discount.
steps: Find the discount = percent × marked price.
To find the percent: discount ÷ marked price × 100%.
Check the sale price is lower than the marked price.
topics.mistake: Adding the discount instead of subtracting it.

topics.title: Commission
topics.note: Commission is a percentage of sales paid to an agent. Commission = rate × sales. Total pay = salary + commission.
steps: If there is a salary, add it to the commission.
To find the rate: commission ÷ sales × 100%.
topics.mistake: Calculating the percentage of the salary instead of the sales.

topics.title: Taxes
topics.note: Tax is a percentage of an amount paid to government. VAT in Nigeria is 7.5% of the price. Price with VAT = price + 7.5% of price.
topics.mistake: Forgetting to add the VAT to the price.

topics.title: Rates
topics.note: A rate is a price per unit. Bill = number of units × rate per unit. Example: 120 units at ₦50 per unit = ₦6,000.
steps: Add up all parts of a bill if there are several.
topics.mistake: Mixing up units (litres, kWh) with money.

topics.title: Rents
topics.note: Rent is the money paid to use a house or shop for a time. Total rent = rent per period × number of periods. Yearly rent ÷ 12 = monthly rent.
steps: Rent per period × number of periods.
topics.mistake: Using months where years are needed.

topics.title: Shares and dividends
topics.note: Shares are parts of a company. Cost = number of shares × price. Dividend is the profit paid to shareholders: a percentage of the value of the shares.
steps: Cost of shares = number × price per share.
Total value = number × value per share.
Dividend per share × number = total dividend.
topics.mistake: Taking the dividend % of the market price instead of the share value.

topics.title: Currency conversion
topics.note: Use the exchange rate. To change to naira, multiply by the rate. To change back, divide by the rate. If 1 US dollar = ₦1,500, then 20 US dollars = ₦30,000.
steps: Write the exchange rate: 1 foreign unit = ₦ ___.
To naira: multiply by the rate.
From naira: divide by the rate.
Check: naira amounts are bigger numbers than foreign amounts.
topics.mistake: Multiplying when you should divide.

topics.title: Powers of numbers
topics.note: A power shows repeated multiplication. $2^5 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32$. The small number is the index (power); the big number is the base.
steps: The base is the number being multiplied.
The index tells how many times it is used.
Multiply the base by itself that many times.
Do powers before multiplying by other numbers.

topics.title: Laws of indices
topics.note: Same base: multiply → add the indices, $a^m × a^n = a^{m+n}$. Divide → subtract, $a^m ÷ a^n = a^{m-n}$. Power of a power → multiply, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$. Also $a^0 = 1$.
steps: Power of a power: multiply indices.
topics.mistake: Multiplying the indices when you should add them.

topics.title: Open sentences
topics.note: An open sentence has a missing number, shown by a letter or box. Find it by doing the opposite operation. n + 7 = 15 → n = 15 − 7 = 8.
steps: Find the missing number in the sentence.
Use the opposite operation to undo what was done.
Put your answer back in to check.
topics.mistake: Doing the same operation instead of its opposite.

topics.title: Linear equations
topics.note: Do the same thing to both sides to get x alone. Undo addition or subtraction first, then undo multiplication or division. 3x + 4 = 19 → 3x = 15 → x = 5.
steps: Get the letter terms on one side.
Whatever you do to one side, do to the other. Check by substituting.
topics.mistake: Changing only one side of the equation.

topics.title: Word problems in open sentences
topics.note: Let a letter stand for the unknown number, write the sentence as an equation, then solve. "A number times 3 plus 5 is 26": 3n + 5 = 26, so n = 7.
steps: Read carefully and let a letter stand for the unknown.
Write the sentence as an equation.
Check the answer fits the story.
topics.mistake: Choosing the wrong operation for words like "less than".

topics.title: Length
topics.note: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 m = 100 cm; 1 cm = 10 mm. To change to a smaller unit, multiply. To change to a bigger unit, divide.
steps: Know the ladder: km → m → cm → mm (×1,000, ×100, ×10).
Going to a smaller unit: multiply.
Going to a bigger unit: divide.
Make units the same before adding.
topics.mistake: Adding numbers with different units.

topics.title: Perimeter of regular plane shapes
topics.note: Perimeter is the distance round a shape. Square: 4 × side. Rectangle: 2 × (length + width). Regular polygon: number of sides × one side.
steps: Perimeter is the distance round the shape.
Regular polygon: number of sides × one side.
topics.mistake: Giving area units for a perimeter.

topics.title: Perimeter of irregular plane shapes
topics.note: Add the lengths of all the sides. For an L-shape, find any missing sides first. Cutting a corner out of a rectangle does not change the perimeter.
steps: For a cut-out corner, the perimeter equals that of the full rectangle.
topics.mistake: Missing a side or adding an inside line.

topics.title: Area of squares
topics.note: Area of a square = side × side. A square of side 6 cm has area 36 cm². Area is measured in square units.
steps: To find the side from area: take the square root.
Cost = area × price per square unit.
topics.mistake: Using the perimeter formula.

topics.title: Area of rectangles
topics.note: Area = length × width. A rectangle 8 m by 5 m has area 40 m². Length = area ÷ width.
topics.mistake: Adding length and width instead of multiplying.

topics.title: Area of parallelograms
topics.note: Area = base × perpendicular height. The height is the straight-up distance between the parallel sides, not the slanted side.
steps: Find the base and the perpendicular height.
Do not use the slanted side as the height.
topics.mistake: Using the slanted side as the height.

topics.title: Area of trapeziums
topics.note: Area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height. Parallel sides 6 and 10, height 4: ½ × 16 × 4 = 32.
topics.mistake: Using a slanted side as the height.

topics.title: Area of circles
topics.note: Area = $\pi r^2$. Use π = 22/7 (or 3.14). Radius 7 cm: $\frac{22}{7} × 7 × 7 = 154$ cm². Radius = half of the diameter.
steps: Use π = 22/7 when the radius is a multiple of 7, or 3.14.
topics.mistake: Using the diameter in place of the radius.

topics.title: Area of irregular plane shapes
topics.note: Split the shape into rectangles and triangles, find each area and add. Or find the area of the big rectangle and subtract the missing part.
steps: Split the shape into rectangles, triangles or squares.
Find the area of each part.
Add them up (or subtract a cut-out).
topics.mistake: Overlapping parts counted twice.

topics.title: Pythagoras rule
topics.note: In a right-angled triangle, hypotenuse² = side² + side². Sides 3 and 4: 9 + 16 = 25, so the hypotenuse is 5. Famous sets: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17.
steps: Find the hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle).
Longest side: add the squares then take the root. Shorter side: subtract the squares then take the root.
topics.mistake: Adding the squares when finding a shorter side.

topics.title: Weight and mass
topics.note: 1 kg = 1,000 g; 1 tonne = 1,000 kg. Multiply to change to a smaller unit, divide to change to a bigger unit.
steps: Use the same unit before adding.
topics.mistake: Mixing kg and g.

topics.title: Volume of cubes
topics.note: Volume = side × side × side. A cube of edge 4 cm has volume 64 cm³. Volume is measured in cubic units.
steps: To find the edge: use the cube root.
Surface area of a cube = 6 × side².
topics.mistake: Confusing volume with surface area.

topics.title: Volume of cuboids
topics.note: Volume = length × width × height. 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm = 60 cm³. Height = volume ÷ (length × width).
steps: All sides in the same unit.
topics.mistake: Adding the sides instead of multiplying.

topics.title: Volume of cylinders
topics.note: Volume = $\pi r^2 h$ (area of the circle × height). With π = 22/7, r = 7 cm and h = 10 cm: $\frac{22}{7} × 49 × 10 = 1,540$ cm³.
steps: Area of the circular base = πr².
topics.mistake: Using the diameter instead of the radius.

topics.title: Volume of triangular prisms
topics.note: Volume = area of the triangle × length of the prism = $\frac{1}{2} b h × l$.
steps: Find the area of the triangle: ½ × base × height.
Multiply by the length of the prism.
Make sure "height" is the triangle height, not the prism length.
topics.mistake: Forgetting the ½ in the triangle area.

topics.title: Capacity
topics.note: Capacity is how much a container holds. 1 litre = 1,000 ml, and 1,000 cm³ = 1 litre. Volume in cm³ ÷ 1,000 gives litres.
steps: Find the volume in cm³ if given dimensions.
Multiply litres by 1,000 to get ml.
topics.mistake: Dividing by 100 instead of 1,000.

topics.title: Binary numbers
topics.note: Binary (base 2) uses only 0 and 1. Place values from the right are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 ... Computers use binary.
steps: Binary uses only the digits 0 and 1.
Each place is double the one on its right.
topics.mistake: Using digits like 2 or 3 in a binary number.

topics.title: Denary numbers
topics.note: Denary (base 10) uses the digits 0 to 9. Each place is 10 times the place on its right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands.
steps: Denary is our everyday base 10 system.
Each place is 10 times the one on its right.
Write the value of each digit and add.
topics.mistake: Mixing the place name with the value.

topics.title: Conversion from binary to denary
topics.note: Write the place values under the digits and add those that have a 1. 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
steps: Write the place values (1, 2, 4, 8 ...) from the right.
Add the place values of the 1s.
topics.mistake: Reading the place values from the left.

topics.title: Conversion from denary to binary
topics.note: Divide by 2 repeatedly and write the remainders. Read them from the bottom up. 13: 13 ÷ 2 = 6 r 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. So 13 = 1101.
steps: Divide the number by 2; write the remainder.
Divide the quotient by 2 again; write the remainder.
Read the remainders from bottom to top.
topics.mistake: Reading the remainders from top to bottom.

topics.title: Addition of binary numbers
topics.note: Add column by column from the right. 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=10 (write 0, carry 1). 101 + 11 = 1000.
topics.mistake: Writing 1 + 1 = 2.

topics.title: Subtraction of binary numbers
topics.note: Subtract column by column. When 0 − 1, borrow from the next column (the borrowed 1 is worth 2). Check by converting to denary.
steps: 0−1: borrow from the next 1 (it is worth 2).
topics.mistake: Borrowing 10 as in denary instead of 2.

lesson.title: Perimeter and Area
lesson.summary: Perimeter and area of rectangles, squares, triangles, parallelograms, trapeziums and circles.
objectives: Find the perimeter of plane shapes
Find the area of rectangles, squares, triangles, parallelograms, trapeziums and circles
Solve fencing and covering word problems
lesson.html:
1. Perimeter and area

Perimeter is the distance around a shape (measured in cm, m). Area is the space inside a shape (measured in cm², m²).

2. Rectangle

Perimeter = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (8 + 5) = 26 cm.
Area = length × width = 8 × 5 = 40 cm².

3. Square

Perimeter = 4 × side. Area = side × side.

4. Triangle

Area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 10 × 6 = 30 cm². The height is the straight (perpendicular) line to the base.

5. Parallelogram and trapezium

Parallelogram: Area = base × perpendicular height.
Trapezium: Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height.

6. Circle

Use π = 22/7 (or 3.14 if told). Circumference = π × diameter. Area = π × radius × radius.
Radius 7 cm: area = 22/7 × 7 × 7 = 154 cm².

7. Word problems

Fencing a farm uses perimeter. Tiling or painting a floor uses area.

Common Entrance tip: Write the units. Perimeter has plain units (cm), area has square units (cm²).

topics.title: Angles
topics.note: An angle is the turn between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees. Acute is less than 90°, right is 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°, straight is 180° and reflex is more than 180°.
steps: Read the size of the angle in degrees.
Name the type (acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex).
Complementary angles add up to 90°; supplementary angles add up to 180°.
topics.mistake: Calling a 180° angle obtuse. 180° is a straight angle.

topics.title: Lines
topics.note: Parallel lines never meet. Perpendicular lines meet at exactly 90°. Intersecting lines cross each other. The midpoint of a line is exactly halfway along it.
steps: Look at how the lines meet or whether they meet.
If they meet at 90° they are perpendicular.
If they stay the same distance apart they are parallel.
topics.mistake: Thinking perpendicular lines must be vertical and horizontal.

topics.title: Parallel lines
topics.note: When a line (transversal) crosses two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add up to 180°.
steps: Spot the parallel lines and the transversal.
Corresponding (F shape) and alternate (Z shape) angles are equal.
Co-interior (C or U shape) angles add up to 180°.
Write an equation and solve for the unknown.
topics.mistake: Using equal angles for co-interior angles.

topics.title: Transversal lines
topics.note: Where two lines cross, vertically opposite angles are equal and angles next to each other on a straight line add up to 180°.
steps: Opposite it (the X shape) is an equal angle.
Next to it on a straight line is 180° minus it.
Use these to find all four angles.
topics.mistake: Thinking adjacent angles are equal.

topics.title: Angles on a straight line
topics.note: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°.
steps: If angles are like x and 2x, add them as 3x = 180°.
Check that all angles add to 180°.
topics.mistake: Using 360° for a straight line.

topics.title: Angles at a point
topics.note: Angles around a point add up to 360° (a full turn).
steps: Add all the angles you know.
For equal angles divide 360° by how many.
topics.mistake: Using 180° instead of 360°.

topics.title: Compass directions
topics.note: The 8 compass points are N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW. Each step is 45°, a quarter turn is 90° and opposite directions are 180° apart.
steps: Picture the compass with North at the top.
Clockwise turns go N → E → S → W.
Each 90° turn moves 2 points; each 45° turn moves 1 point.
topics.mistake: Turning anticlockwise when the question says clockwise.

topics.title: Bearings
topics.note: A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from North, written with three figures. North = 000°, East = 090°, South = 180°, West = 270°. A back bearing is 180° more or less.
steps: Turn clockwise to the direction you want.
Write the angle with three figures (045°, not 45°).
Back bearing: add 180° if less than 180°, otherwise subtract 180°.
topics.mistake: Measuring anticlockwise or leaving off the leading zero.

topics.title: Polygons
topics.note: A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides. Interior angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles of any polygon add up to 360°. Diagonals = n(n − 3) ÷ 2.
steps: Use the formula that matches the question.
For a regular polygon each interior angle = sum ÷ n.
topics.mistake: Using n × 180° instead of (n − 2) × 180°.

topics.title: Triangles
topics.note: A triangle has 3 sides and its angles add up to 180°. Equilateral: 3 equal sides. Isosceles: 2 equal sides (and 2 equal angles). Scalene: no equal sides.
steps: Subtract from 180° to get the third angle.
Name the triangle by its sides or angles.
In an isosceles triangle, base angles are equal.
topics.mistake: Forgetting that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.

topics.title: Quadrilaterals
topics.note: A quadrilateral has 4 sides and its angles add up to 360°. Square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, trapezium and kite are all quadrilaterals.
steps: Subtract from 360° to get the missing angle.
Use the properties: a rhombus has 4 equal sides, a parallelogram has opposite sides parallel.
topics.mistake: Using 180° (the triangle total) for a quadrilateral.

topics.title: Pentagons
topics.note: A pentagon has 5 sides. Its interior angles add up to 540°. Each angle of a regular pentagon is 108°.
steps: For a regular pentagon divide 540° by 5.
Perimeter of a regular pentagon: 5 × side.
topics.mistake: Using 360° for the angle sum.

topics.title: Hexagons
topics.note: A hexagon has 6 sides. Its interior angles add up to 720°. Each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°.
steps: For a regular hexagon divide 720° by 6.
Perimeter of a regular hexagon: 6 × side.
topics.mistake: Mixing up hexagon (6) with pentagon (5).

topics.title: Octagons
topics.note: An octagon has 8 sides. Its interior angles add up to 1,080°. Each angle of a regular octagon is 135°.
steps: For a regular octagon divide 1,080° by 8.
Perimeter of a regular octagon: 8 × side.
topics.mistake: Mixing up octagon (8) with hexagon (6).

topics.title: Time
topics.note: There are 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 24 hours in a day. In 24-hour time, p.m. hours add 12. Add or subtract hours and minutes separately.
steps: To change to 24-hour time: p.m. add 12 (except 12 noon).
To add a duration: add hours, then minutes (60 minutes = 1 hour).
To find a duration: subtract the start from the end.
topics.mistake: Treating 60 minutes as 100 minutes.

topics.title: Distance
topics.note: Distance = speed × time. Speed = distance ÷ time. Time = distance ÷ speed. Use matching units (km and hours, or m and seconds).
steps: Write down what is given: distance, speed or time.
Choose the formula (use the distance-speed-time triangle).
Change minutes to hours if the speed is in km/h.
Write the unit in the answer.
topics.mistake: Not changing minutes to hours.

topics.title: Average speed
topics.note: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. It is not the average of the speeds, unless the times are equal.
steps: Divide total distance by total time.
topics.mistake: Adding the speeds and dividing by 2.

topics.title: Collection of data
topics.note: Data is information collected by counting, measuring, asking questions (questionnaire or survey), interviewing or observing.
steps: Decide what you want to find out.
Choose how to collect the data (questionnaire, interview, observation).
Organise the data in a tally or table.
topics.mistake: Counting some answers twice or missing some out.

topics.title: Tallying data
topics.note: A tally uses strokes to count. Every fifth stroke crosses the four before it, so each group stands for 5.
steps: Make one stroke for each item.
Cross the four strokes for every fifth item.
Count in fives, then add the single strokes.
Write the total in a frequency table.
topics.mistake: Counting each group as 4 instead of 5.

topics.title: Frequency tables
topics.note: A frequency table shows how many times each value occurs. The total frequency is the number of items counted.
steps: List the values in one column.
Write the frequency (count) in the next column.
Add the frequencies to get the total.
Multiply value × frequency to find totals.
topics.mistake: Adding the values instead of the frequencies.

topics.title: Bar charts
topics.note: A bar chart uses bars of equal width. The height of each bar shows the frequency. It is easy to compare categories.
steps: Read the labels under the bars.
Read the height of the bar on the scale.
To find a total, add all the bars.
topics.mistake: Reading the wrong scale or the wrong bar.

topics.title: Histograms
topics.note: A histogram shows grouped data (class intervals). The bars touch and the height shows the frequency of each class.
steps: Read the class intervals on the bottom.
Read the height of each bar for its frequency.
The tallest bar is the modal class.
Add all the bars for the total frequency.
topics.mistake: Treating a histogram like a bar chart with gaps and separate categories.

topics.title: Pie charts
topics.note: A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors. Each sector angle = (part ÷ total) × 360°. The sectors add up to 360°.
steps: Or find the share from the angle: (angle ÷ 360°) × total.
Check the angles add up to 360°.
topics.mistake: Forgetting to multiply by 360°.

topics.title: Mean
topics.note: The mean (average) = sum of all the values ÷ number of values.
steps: Count how many values there are.
Divide the sum by the count.
To find a missing value: total = mean × count, then subtract the others.
topics.mistake: Dividing by the wrong number of values.

topics.title: Median
topics.note: The median is the middle value when the numbers are arranged in order.
steps: Arrange the numbers from smallest to biggest.
If there are two middle values, add them and divide by 2.
Check you used all the numbers.
topics.mistake: Not arranging the numbers in order first.

topics.title: Mode
topics.note: The mode is the value that appears most often. A set can have two modes, or no mode if every value appears once.
steps: Write the numbers in order (this helps).
The one with the highest count is the mode.
If all appear once, there is no mode.
topics.mistake: Choosing the biggest number instead of the most frequent.

topics.title: Probability
topics.note: Probability tells how likely an event is. P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes. It is between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
steps: Write favourable ÷ total as a fraction.
topics.mistake: Putting the numbers the wrong way round (total over favourable).

topics.title: Common and proper nouns
topics.note: A noun is a naming word. A common noun names any person, place, animal or thing. A proper noun names one particular person, place or thing and always starts with a capital letter.
steps: Find the nouns: Ngozi, rice, Ifo, market.
Which names ONE particular person or place? Ngozi and Ifo.
topics.mistake: Writing a proper noun with a small letter, such as "lagos" instead of "Lagos".

topics.title: Abstract and concrete nouns
topics.note: A concrete noun names something you can see or touch. An abstract noun names a feeling, quality or idea that you cannot touch.
steps: It is a quality of a person.
So it is an abstract noun.
topics.mistake: Thinking that "hunger" or "health" can be touched. They are feelings or states, so they are abstract.

topics.title: Collective nouns
topics.note: A collective noun is the name of a group of people, animals or things taken together as one.
steps: The group name for lions is "pride".
topics.mistake: Using the wrong group name, such as "a herd of fish". Learn each pair together.

topics.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
topics.note: Countable nouns can be counted one by one (one book, two books). Uncountable nouns cannot be counted that way (water, rice, advice).
topics.mistake: Writing "advices" or "informations". These nouns have no plural.

topics.title: Singular and plural nouns
topics.note: Singular means one; plural means more than one. Most nouns add -s, but some follow special rules.
steps: Change y to i and add es.
topics.mistake: Writing "childs" or "mans". Learn the irregular plurals by heart.

topics.title: Gender of nouns
topics.note: Gender tells whether a noun is masculine (male), feminine (female), common (either) or neuter (a thing).
topics.mistake: Calling "teacher" or "doctor" masculine. These are common gender.

topics.title: Possessive nouns
topics.note: A possessive noun shows who owns something. We use an apostrophe.
steps: Teachers is plural and ends in s.
topics.mistake: Writing "the boys ball" with no apostrophe, or "mango's" for the plural.

topics.title: Personal pronouns
topics.note: A pronoun takes the place of a noun. Personal pronouns stand for people or things: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (subject) and me, him, her, us, them (object).
steps: The pronoun comes after "to", so it is an object.
topics.mistake: Saying "Me and Tunde went to the market." Say "Tunde and I went".

topics.title: Possessive pronouns
topics.note: A possessive pronoun shows ownership and stands alone: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs.
steps: The possessive pronoun for me is "mine".
topics.mistake: Writing "yours's", "her's" or "our's". These never have an apostrophe.

topics.title: Reflexive pronouns
topics.note: A reflexive pronoun ends in -self or -selves. It shows that the doer and the receiver of an action are the same person.
steps: Bola is the doer and the receiver.
topics.mistake: Writing "themself" or "hisself".

topics.title: Relative pronouns
topics.note: A relative pronoun joins a describing part to a noun: who, whom, whose, which, that.
steps: The word refers to a person.
topics.mistake: Using "which" for people.

topics.title: Demonstrative and interrogative pronouns
topics.note: Demonstrative pronouns point out things: this, that, these, those. Interrogative pronouns ask questions: who, whom, whose, which, what.
steps: Books is plural and far away.
topics.mistake: Using "this" for plural things: write "these books", not "this books".

topics.title: Action and linking verbs
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: A verb tells what someone does or is. Action verbs show an action; linking verbs join the subject to a describing word.
topics.mistake: Thinking every verb shows action.

topics.title: Auxiliary verbs
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: An auxiliary (helping) verb comes before the main verb to help it show tense or make questions and negatives.
topics.mistake: Using the wrong form: "Tunde have finished". Use "has".

topics.title: Modal verbs
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: Modal verbs are special helping verbs that show ability, permission, possibility, duty or advice: can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would.
steps: This is a rule or duty.
topics.mistake: Adding -s or -ing after a modal: "can swims", "must going".

topics.title: Transitive and intransitive verbs
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: A transitive verb needs an object to complete its meaning. An intransitive verb does not.
topics.mistake: Thinking that an adverb such as "loudly" is an object.

topics.title: Regular and irregular verbs
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: Regular verbs make their past tense and past participle by adding -ed or -d. Irregular verbs change in other ways.
topics.mistake: Writing "goed", "buyed" or "eated".

topics.title: Adjectives
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: An adjective describes a noun or pronoun. It tells what kind, how many or which one.
steps: The nouns are Tunde and bag.
topics.mistake: Confusing an adjective with the noun it describes.

topics.title: Degrees of comparison
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: Adjectives have three degrees: positive (tall), comparative (taller) and superlative (tallest).
topics.mistake: Writing "more taller" or "goodest".

topics.title: Adverbs of manner, time and place
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: An adverb tells more about a verb: how (manner), when (time) or where (place) something happens.
topics.mistake: Using the adjective "good" where the adverb "well" is needed: He sings good.

topics.title: Adverbs of frequency and degree
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: Adverbs of frequency tell how often. Adverbs of degree tell how much.
topics.mistake: Placing "always" after the main verb: "He goes always". Say "He always goes".

topics.title: Prepositions of place and time
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: A preposition shows the relation of a noun to another word, such as place or time.
topics.mistake: Saying "in Monday" or "at June".

topics.title: Prepositions of direction
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: Prepositions of direction show movement: to, into, onto, through, across, along, towards, up, down, out of.
steps: He went from one side to the other.
topics.mistake: Mixing "in" (place) and "into" (movement).

topics.title: Conjunctions
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses: and, but, or, so, because, although, when, if, unless, until.
steps: Eating is the result of hunger.
topics.mistake: Using "but" and "although" together in one sentence.

topics.title: Interjections
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: An interjection is a word or short phrase that shows a sudden strong feeling. It is usually followed by an exclamation mark.
topics.mistake: Joining an interjection to the sentence without a mark: Wow it is big.

topics.title: Articles and determiners
topics.strand: Verbs, Adjectives, Adverbs and Other Word Classes
topics.note: Articles are a, an and the. Determiners come before a noun to show how many or which one: some, any, many, much, few, each, every.
steps: Umbrella begins with a vowel sound.
topics.mistake: Writing "an university" - it begins with a consonant sound.

topics.title: Simple present
topics.note: The simple present tense tells about habits, facts and things that are always true.
topics.mistake: Forgetting -s: "She go to school".

topics.title: Present continuous
topics.note: The present continuous tense tells about an action happening now.
topics.mistake: Leaving out the helping verb: "Ada reading now".

topics.title: Present perfect
topics.note: The present perfect tense links the past to now. It tells about an action that has just finished or whose result matters now.
steps: The participle of eat is eaten.
topics.mistake: Saying "has ate" instead of "has eaten".

topics.title: Simple past
topics.note: The simple past tense tells about actions that finished in the past.
topics.mistake: Using the past form after did: "Did she went?" Say "Did she go?".

topics.title: Past continuous
topics.note: The past continuous tense tells about an action that was going on at a time in the past.
topics.mistake: Using "were" with a singular name.

topics.title: Past perfect
topics.note: The past perfect tense tells about an action completed before another action in the past.
topics.mistake: Using the simple past for both actions.

topics.title: Simple future
topics.note: The simple future tense tells about actions that will happen later.
topics.mistake: Using will + past: "will came".

topics.title: Subject-verb agreement
topics.note: The verb must agree with its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
topics.mistake: Matching the verb to the nearest noun instead of the real subject.

topics.title: Concord with collective nouns
topics.note: A collective noun names a group. When the group acts as one unit it takes a singular verb. Some words like police and cattle are always plural.
steps: The committee acts as one unit.
topics.mistake: Using "are" after every collective noun.

topics.title: Concord with indefinite pronouns
topics.note: Indefinite pronouns do not name a particular person. Most are singular and take singular verbs: everyone, someone, nobody, each, either, neither.
topics.mistake: Using "are" with everyone or "have" with each.

topics.title: Types of sentences
topics.note: Sentences do different jobs. A statement tells, a question asks, a command orders or requests, and an exclamation shows strong feeling.
steps: It tells someone to do something.
topics.mistake: Ending a question with a full stop.

topics.title: Subject and predicate
topics.note: Every sentence has a subject (who or what the sentence is about) and a predicate (what is said about the subject).
topics.mistake: Thinking the subject is always one word.

topics.title: Phrases
topics.note: A phrase is a group of words that does not have its own subject and verb. It acts as one part of a sentence.
steps: So it is a prepositional phrase.
topics.mistake: Calling a phrase a sentence.

topics.title: Clauses
topics.note: A clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb. A main (independent) clause makes sense alone; a dependent clause does not.
topics.mistake: Treating a dependent clause as a full sentence.

topics.title: Simple, compound and complex sentences
topics.note: Sentences can be simple, compound or complex depending on their clauses.
topics.mistake: Calling every long sentence compound.

topics.title: Question tags
topics.note: A question tag is a short question added to a statement to ask for agreement.
steps: Use a negative tag: can't she?
topics.mistake: Using the wrong pronoun in the tag.

topics.title: Direct speech
topics.note: Direct speech gives the exact words a person said, inside speech marks.
steps: Put speech marks round the spoken words with the full stop inside.
topics.mistake: Putting the full stop outside the speech marks.

topics.title: Indirect speech
topics.note: Indirect (reported) speech tells what someone said without using their exact words or speech marks.
topics.mistake: Forgetting to move the tense back.

topics.title: Active and passive voice
topics.note: In the active voice the doer comes first. In the passive voice the receiver of the action comes first.
topics.mistake: Using the past tense instead of the participle: "was broke".

topics.title: Conditional sentences
topics.note: Conditional sentences say what happens if something is true. They have an "if" clause and a result clause.
topics.mistake: Using "will" in the if clause: "If it will rain".

topics.title: Negatives and questions
topics.note: We make negatives with not and questions by moving or adding a helping verb.
steps: Use does with a singular name.
topics.mistake: Keeping the -s after does: "Does she sings?".

topics.title: Word order and jumbled sentences
topics.note: English sentences follow a usual order: subject, verb, then object or other details. Jumbled words must be put back in sense.
topics.mistake: Putting the verb before the subject.

topics.title: Synonyms
topics.note: Synonyms are words with the same or almost the same meaning.
topics.mistake: Choosing a word that only looks similar.

topics.title: Antonyms
topics.note: Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.
topics.mistake: Choosing a word that is only different, not opposite.

topics.title: Homophones
topics.note: Homophones are words that sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.
topics.mistake: Writing "their" for "there".

topics.title: Homonyms
topics.note: Homonyms are words spelt the same but with different meanings.
topics.mistake: Picking the first meaning that comes to mind without using the sentence.

topics.title: Prefixes
topics.note: A prefix is a group of letters added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning.
topics.mistake: Using in- before p: write "impossible", not "inpossible".

topics.title: Suffixes
topics.note: A suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning or word class.
topics.mistake: Writing "happyness" instead of "happiness".

topics.title: Root and compound words
topics.note: A root word is the main part of a word. A compound word joins two whole words to make a new word.
topics.mistake: Cutting off the wrong part of a word.

topics.title: Word formation
topics.note: We can make new words by changing a word's ending to turn it into a noun, verb, adjective or adverb.
topics.mistake: Using the wrong ending.

topics.title: Idioms
topics.note: An idiom is a group of words with a special meaning that is different from the meaning of each word.
steps: It means to reveal a secret.
topics.mistake: Explaining an idiom by its separate words.

topics.title: Proverbs
topics.note: A proverb is a short wise saying that gives advice or tells a truth.
topics.mistake: Taking a proverb literally.

topics.title: Collocations
topics.note: Collocations are words that naturally go together.
steps: The usual phrase is "make a mistake".
topics.mistake: Saying "do a mistake" or "make homework".

topics.title: One-word substitutes
topics.note: A one-word substitute is a single word that replaces a long group of words.
topics.mistake: Choosing a word that is only related.

topics.title: Words often confused
topics.note: Some words look or sound alike but have different meanings. We must choose the right one.
steps: After "some", we need the noun: advice.
topics.mistake: Mixing up the noun and the verb pair.

topics.title: Spelling rules
topics.note: Spelling rules help us write words correctly.
steps: Make ends with a silent e.
topics.mistake: Writing "recieve" or "makeing".

topics.title: Abbreviations and contractions
topics.note: An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word or phrase. A contraction joins two words with an apostrophe.
steps: N is National; Y is Youth.
S is Service; C is Corps.
topics.mistake: Putting the apostrophe in the wrong place: "do'nt".

topics.title: Everyday vocabulary
topics.note: Everyday vocabulary means words for the things around us: fruits, jobs, places, body parts, transport.
topics.mistake: Mixing words from different groups.

topics.title: Dictionary skills
topics.note: A dictionary lists words in alphabetical order with their meanings, parts of speech and pronunciation.
steps: Compare the second letter: a comes before o.
topics.mistake: Ignoring the second letter when words start the same.

topics.title: Vowel sounds
topics.note: Vowel sounds are made with an open mouth and no blocking of air. English has 12 pure vowel sounds, some short and some long.
topics.mistake: Trusting spelling instead of sound.

topics.title: Consonant sounds
topics.note: Consonant sounds are made when the air is blocked or squeezed in the mouth. Some letters make different sounds.
topics.mistake: Thinking the same letter always has the same sound.

topics.title: Diphthongs
topics.note: A diphthong is a vowel sound made of two sounds glided together.
topics.mistake: Treating a diphthong as a single short vowel.

topics.title: Syllables
topics.note: A syllable is a beat in a word. Each syllable has one vowel sound.
topics.mistake: Counting letters instead of beats.

topics.title: Word stress
topics.note: In words with more than one syllable, one syllable is said louder and longer. That is the stressed syllable.
topics.mistake: Stressing the wrong syllable.

topics.title: Rhymes
topics.note: Words rhyme when their endings sound the same.
topics.mistake: Matching spelling instead of sound.

topics.title: Sentence stress
topics.note: In a sentence, important words are stressed and small grammar words are weak.
topics.mistake: Stressing every word equally.

topics.title: Intonation
topics.note: Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice when we speak.
topics.mistake: Using a falling tone for yes/no questions.

topics.title: Similar-sounding words
topics.note: Some words sound almost alike. Hearing the small difference helps us speak and spell correctly.
topics.mistake: Choosing the word that merely sounds right.

topics.title: Silent letters
topics.note: A silent letter is written but not pronounced.
topics.mistake: Pronouncing the silent letter.

topics.title: Main idea
topics.note: The main idea is what a passage is mostly about. Details support it.
steps: The whole passage is about a lost bag.
Choose a title that covers all of it.
topics.mistake: Choosing a detail instead of the whole idea.

topics.title: Details and facts
topics.note: Details and facts are the exact pieces of information a passage gives: who, what, where, when, why and how many.
topics.mistake: Answering from memory instead of the passage.

topics.title: Inference
topics.note: To infer is to work out something the writer does not say directly, using clues.
topics.mistake: Choosing a guess that has no clue in the text.

topics.title: Context clues
topics.note: Context clues are the words around an unknown word that help you work out its meaning.
topics.mistake: Looking at the word alone.

topics.title: Fact and opinion
topics.note: A fact can be proved true. An opinion tells what someone thinks or feels.
topics.mistake: Treating a strong feeling as a fact.

topics.title: Sequencing events
topics.note: Sequencing means putting events or steps in the correct order.
topics.mistake: Putting the last step first.

topics.title: Narrative passages
topics.note: A narrative passage tells a story with characters, a setting, a problem and a solution.
topics.mistake: Mixing up the problem and the solution.

topics.title: Descriptive passages
topics.note: A descriptive passage paints a picture with words, using details that appeal to the senses.
topics.mistake: Ignoring some of the clues.

topics.title: Cloze passages
topics.note: A cloze passage has gaps. You choose the word that fits best in meaning and grammar.
steps: A doctor works where people are treated.
topics.mistake: Choosing a word that fits the grammar but not the meaning.

topics.title: Summary skills
topics.note: A summary is a short account of the main points of a passage in your own words.
steps: A summary keeps the main points.
topics.mistake: Copying whole sentences.

topics.title: Notices, charts and signs
topics.note: Notices, timetables, charts and signs give information quickly. Read them carefully.
topics.mistake: Reading the wrong row or column.

topics.title: Capital letters
topics.note: Capital letters mark the start of sentences and the names of special things.
topics.mistake: Writing a day or place with a small letter.

topics.title: Full stops, question and exclamation marks
topics.note: Every sentence ends with a mark: a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark.
topics.mistake: Ending a question with a full stop.

topics.title: Commas
topics.note: A comma is a short pause in a sentence. It separates parts to make meaning clear.
topics.mistake: Putting a comma before the last "and" in a short list in this style or adding too many commas.

topics.title: Apostrophes
topics.note: An apostrophe shows ownership or replaces missing letters.
topics.mistake: Writing "its" for "it's".

topics.title: Quotation marks
topics.note: Quotation (speech) marks show the exact words someone says.
topics.mistake: Putting the full stop outside the speech marks.

topics.title: Colons, semicolons and hyphens
topics.note: A colon introduces a list. A semicolon joins related sentences. A hyphen joins words.
topics.mistake: Using a colon in the wrong place.

topics.title: Paragraphs
topics.note: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea.
topics.mistake: Putting two ideas in one paragraph.

topics.title: Narrative essay
topics.note: A narrative essay tells a story in the past tense.
topics.mistake: Switching between tenses.

topics.title: Descriptive essay
topics.note: A descriptive essay paints a picture using the five senses and vivid adjectives.
topics.mistake: Writing a story instead of a description.

topics.title: Expository essay
topics.note: An expository essay explains or informs using facts and examples.
topics.mistake: Telling a story instead of explaining.

topics.title: Argumentative essay
topics.note: An argumentative essay gives reasons to support a point of view and answers the opposite view.
topics.mistake: Giving only opinion without reasons.

topics.title: Informal letter
topics.note: An informal letter is written to a friend or relative in a friendly tone.
topics.mistake: Using "Yours faithfully".

topics.title: Formal letter
topics.note: A formal letter is written to an official, a principal or a company in a polite tone.
topics.mistake: Using slang or an informal tone.

topics.title: Speech writing
topics.note: A speech is written to be spoken to an audience.
topics.mistake: Forgetting to greet the audience.

topics.title: Report writing
topics.note: A report gives facts about an event or investigation in a formal way.
topics.mistake: Adding personal feelings.

topics.title: Editing and proofreading
topics.note: Proofreading means checking writing for mistakes and correcting them.
topics.mistake: Reading too fast and missing mistakes.

topics.title: Poetry basics
topics.note: A poem is written in lines and stanzas, often with rhyme and rhythm.
topics.mistake: Confusing a line with a stanza.

topics.title: Simile
topics.note: A simile compares two things using like or as.
topics.mistake: Calling a metaphor a simile.

topics.title: Metaphor
topics.note: A metaphor says one thing is another, without like or as.
topics.mistake: Taking it literally.

topics.title: Personification
topics.note: Personification gives human actions or feelings to animals, things or ideas.
topics.mistake: Missing the human action word.

topics.title: Hyperbole and irony
topics.note: Hyperbole is a big exaggeration. Irony shows the opposite of what is expected or said.
topics.mistake: Taking hyperbole literally.

topics.title: Onomatopoeia and alliteration
topics.note: Onomatopoeia words sound like what they mean. Alliteration repeats the same beginning sound.
topics.mistake: Confusing alliteration with rhyme.

topics.title: Characters
topics.note: Characters are the people or animals in a story. Their actions show what they are like.
topics.mistake: Judging only by what a character says.

topics.title: Plot and setting
topics.note: Plot is the order of events. Setting is the time and place.
steps: A hot afternoon in a village.
topics.mistake: Mixing setting and plot.

topics.title: Theme and moral lessons
topics.note: A theme is the main message of a story. A moral is a lesson about how to behave.
topics.mistake: Retelling the story instead of giving the lesson.

topics.title: Drama basics
topics.note: Drama is a story written to be acted on a stage, using dialogue and stage directions.
topics.mistake: Reading stage directions aloud.

topics.title: Living and non-living things
topics.note: Living things (organisms) grow, feed, breathe, move, sense changes, make waste and reproduce. Non-living things do none of these things.
steps: Does it reproduce with spores? Yes.
topics.mistake: Thinking that anything that moves is living. A car and a river move but are not alive.

topics.title: Characteristics of living things
topics.note: All living things carry out seven life processes: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition (remember MRS GREN).
steps: A tree becomes taller and wider.
An increase in size is called growth.
topics.mistake: Saying plants do not move or breathe. Plants move parts of their body slowly and respire all the time.

topics.title: Classification of living things
topics.note: Classification means sorting living things into groups by features they share. The two big groups are plants and animals, with fungi and microorganisms too.
steps: It has fur and feeds its young on milk.
topics.mistake: Thinking a bat is a bird because it flies. A bat has fur and feeds its young milk, so it is a mammal.

topics.title: Parts of a plant and their functions
topics.note: A flowering plant has roots, a stem, leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. Each part has its own job.
steps: The part in the soil is the root.
topics.mistake: Saying the leaves take in water from the soil. Roots do that; leaves make food.

topics.title: Flowering and non-flowering plants
topics.note: Flowering plants make flowers, fruits and seeds. Non-flowering plants, like ferns, mosses and pine trees, do not make flowers.
topics.mistake: Thinking a pine tree has flowers. Pine seeds grow in cones.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.note: Photosynthesis is how green plants make food. Using sunlight, they change carbon dioxide and water into sugar (glucose) and give out oxygen.
steps: They release the other gas, oxygen.
topics.mistake: Saying plants take in oxygen for photosynthesis. They take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.

topics.title: Reproduction in plants
topics.note: Flowering plants reproduce by seeds. Pollen moves to the stigma (pollination), the male and female cells join (fertilisation), and the ovule becomes a seed. Some plants also grow from stems or tubers.
topics.mistake: Confusing pollination with fertilisation. Pollination is the carrying of pollen; fertilisation is the joining of cells.

topics.title: Seed germination
topics.note: Germination is the growth of a seed into a young plant. A seed needs water, air (oxygen) and a suitable warmth. It does not need light until the leaves grow.
topics.mistake: Saying seeds need light to germinate. They need water, air and warmth.

topics.title: Vertebrates and invertebrates
topics.note: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone: mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians. Invertebrates have no backbone: insects, spiders, worms, snails and crabs.
steps: Does it have a backbone? No.
It has a soft body and shell.
topics.mistake: Thinking that a spider is an insect. A spider has eight legs and is not an insect.

topics.title: Animal life cycles
topics.note: A life cycle is the series of changes an animal goes through from birth to adulthood and death. Some insects change body form completely (metamorphosis).
steps: The pupa changes into the adult.
topics.mistake: Missing out the pupa stage. A butterfly passes through egg, larva, pupa and adult.

topics.title: Adaptation of plants and animals
topics.note: An adaptation is a feature or behaviour that helps a plant or animal to live well in its habitat.
topics.mistake: Thinking an adaptation happens in one animal in one day. Adaptations are features that pass from parents to young over many generations.

topics.title: Skeleton and joints
topics.note: The skeleton is the frame of bones that supports the body, protects soft organs and works with muscles to move us. Bones meet at joints.
steps: The elbow bends and straightens only.
topics.mistake: Mixing up ligaments and tendons. Ligaments join bones; tendons join muscles to bones.

topics.title: Muscles and body movement
topics.note: Muscles are tissues that can contract (get shorter) and relax. They pull on bones to move the body. Muscles work in pairs.
topics.mistake: Thinking muscles push bones. Muscles only pull, so they work in pairs.

topics.title: Digestive system
topics.note: Digestion breaks food into small soluble pieces the blood can carry. Food passes through the mouth, gullet, stomach, small intestine and large intestine.
steps: Food is digested in the stomach and small intestine.
Absorption is mostly in the small intestine.
topics.mistake: Saying most absorption is in the stomach. It is in the small intestine.

topics.title: Teeth and dental care
topics.note: Teeth cut, tear and grind food. Humans have milk teeth (20) and then permanent teeth (32). Brushing and eating well prevent decay.
topics.mistake: Thinking milk teeth do not matter. They hold space for the permanent teeth.

topics.title: Respiratory system
topics.note: Breathing brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. Air passes through the nose, windpipe and bronchi into the lungs.
topics.mistake: Saying we breathe out only carbon dioxide. Exhaled air still has oxygen.

topics.title: Heart and blood circulation
topics.note: The heart pumps blood through arteries, veins and capillaries. Blood carries oxygen, food and waste around the body.
topics.mistake: Saying veins always carry blood without oxygen. This is true for most, but the pulmonary vein carries oxygen-rich blood.

topics.title: Excretory system and the skin
topics.note: Excretion is the removal of waste made by the body. The kidneys make urine, the skin gives out sweat, and the lungs breathe out carbon dioxide.
steps: Waste is taken from the blood.
This is the job of the kidneys.
topics.mistake: Confusing excretion with egestion. Excretion removes waste made by the body; egestion removes undigested food.

topics.title: Nervous system
topics.note: The nervous system controls the body. The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. Nerves carry messages between the body and the brain.
topics.mistake: Thinking reflex actions are controlled by thinking. They happen before the brain decides.

topics.title: Sense organs: sight and hearing
topics.note: The eye detects light so we can see. The ear detects sound so we can hear and also helps us to balance.
steps: Light is focused at the back.
topics.mistake: Saying we see with the lens alone. The brain makes sense of the signals from the retina.

topics.title: Sense organs: smell, taste and touch
topics.note: The nose detects smells, the tongue detects tastes and the skin detects touch, heat, cold and pain. Each sends messages to the brain.
steps: Heat is felt on the body.
topics.mistake: Saying the tongue alone gives the full flavour. Smell helps a lot.

topics.title: Growth and puberty
topics.note: Humans pass through life stages: baby, child, adolescent, adult and old age. Puberty is when the body changes from a child to an adult, usually between ages 10 and 16.
steps: It is a stage of life.
The body changes into an adult body.
topics.mistake: Thinking puberty starts at the same age for everyone. It begins at different times for different people.

topics.title: Human reproduction and life stages
topics.note: Reproduction produces new human beings. A male cell (sperm) joins a female cell (egg cell) in fertilisation. The baby grows in the mother womb for about nine months.
topics.mistake: Thinking a baby breathes in the womb. It gets oxygen from the mother through the placenta.

topics.title: Habitats
topics.note: A habitat is the natural place where a plant or animal lives. It gives food, water, shelter and space.
topics.mistake: Thinking a habitat is only the animal home. It also includes the food, water and shelter around it.

topics.title: Food chains and food webs
topics.note: A food chain shows who eats whom, with arrows pointing the way energy flows. Many food chains linked together form a food web. All energy begins with the Sun.
steps: The first animal, which eats grass.
topics.mistake: Drawing the arrow from the eater to the food. The arrow shows where the energy goes, so it points to the eater.

topics.title: Ecosystems
topics.note: An ecosystem is a community of living things and their non-living surroundings working together. Living parts are biotic; non-living parts are abiotic.
topics.mistake: Thinking an ecosystem has only animals. It includes plants and non-living things too.

topics.title: Soil types
topics.note: Soil is the top layer of the Earth made of rock particles, humus, water and air. The main soil types are sandy, clay and loamy. Loamy soil is best for farming.
steps: It must hold water yet drain.
topics.mistake: Thinking clay drains quickly. Clay particles are tiny and hold water.

topics.title: Soil erosion and conservation
topics.note: Soil erosion is the wearing away and carrying off of topsoil by water or wind. Conserving soil means protecting it from erosion and keeping it fertile.
steps: Leaves reduce the force of rain.
topics.mistake: Thinking only water causes erosion. Wind carries soil too, especially in the dry north.

topics.title: Sources and uses of water
topics.note: Water comes from rain, rivers, streams, springs, wells, boreholes, lakes and the sea. We use it for drinking, cooking, washing, farming, industry and making electricity.
steps: It is drilled into the ground.
topics.mistake: Thinking all clear water is safe. It may still carry germs.

topics.title: The water cycle
topics.note: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the Earth and the air. The Sun heats water so it evaporates, cools into clouds (condensation) and falls as rain (precipitation).
topics.mistake: Saying clouds are made of water vapour. Clouds are tiny drops of liquid water or ice.

topics.title: Water pollution and purification
topics.note: Water pollution is the contamination of water by harmful things. Polluted water must be purified before drinking, by filtering, boiling or adding chlorine.
topics.mistake: Thinking a filter alone removes all germs. Boil or chlorinate after filtering.

topics.title: Air and its composition
topics.note: Air is a mixture of gases: about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen, about 1 percent argon and a little carbon dioxide, water vapour and dust.
topics.mistake: Saying air is mostly oxygen. It is mostly nitrogen.

topics.title: Air pollution
topics.note: Air pollution is harmful substances in the air, such as smoke, fumes and dust. It harms health, plants and the climate.
topics.mistake: Thinking pollution is only smoke you can see. Some gases like carbon monoxide are invisible.

topics.title: Waste management and recycling
topics.note: Waste is anything we throw away. Good waste management follows the 3 Rs: reduce, reuse and recycle. Biodegradable waste rots; non-biodegradable waste does not.
steps: Does it rot in the soil?
topics.mistake: Thinking burying plastic makes it disappear. It stays in the soil for many years.

topics.title: Conservation of natural resources
topics.note: Natural resources are useful things from nature such as water, soil, forests, minerals and wildlife. Conservation means using them wisely so they last. Renewable resources can be replaced; non-renewable resources cannot.
steps: It took millions of years to form.
topics.mistake: Thinking renewable resources can never run out. Trees and fish can be used up if over-harvested.

topics.title: Weather and weather instruments
topics.note: Weather is the state of the air at a place and time: temperature, rain, wind, cloud and sunshine. Weather instruments measure these things.
topics.mistake: Mixing up weather and climate. Weather is for a short time; climate is the average over many years.

topics.title: Climate and climate change
